extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, political science, communication, journalism, and general readers interested in propaganda and social psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles about how stereotypes, codes, and blind spots form, persist, and shape public opinion and observation; includes guidance for recognizing, testing, and countering these mental frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype stamps itself upon evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The stereotype 'stamps itself upon the evidence in the very act of securing the evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that observers carry preconceptions (e.g., travelers who 'carried chiefly his appetite' or impressions of Pullman cars) and these preconceptions shape what evidence is noticed and reported. The stereotype organizes perception as evidence is gathered, so reported facts often reflect the stereotype as much as external reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement when experience matches expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: If what we are looking at corresponds successfully with what we anticipated, the stereotype is reinforced for the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observation fits a stereotype, the mental pattern is strengthened (example: someone who 'knows in advance that the Japanese are cunning' and then meets two dishonest Japanese). This explains why limited confirming instances have outsized influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses to contradictory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When experience contradicts the stereotype, observers either (a) dismiss it as an exception, (b) discredit the witness/find a flaw and forget it, or (c) if open-minded, allow the novelty to modify the stereotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text lists outcomes: pooh-pooh contradiction, discredit witness, forget it, or, if curious and open-minded, incorporate novelty or even invert moral canon (e.g., literary inversion where Judas becomes hero). Use this to evaluate how resilient or revisable a public belief is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes exclude the test of particular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: By asserting a general stereotype (e.g., 'slaves are by nature intended to be slaves'), one excludes the question whether particular instances conform, thus preventing destructive doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle example: declaring slaves are 'by nature' slaves prevents examining whether specific individuals are naturally slaves. Criterion: check whether a generalization is being used to immunize itself from empirical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes act as cognitive economizers but create blind spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes economize attention in a busy life and defend position in society, but they 'censor out much that needs to be taken into account' and create blind spots that can later cause serious error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for saving time and focusing action, but when the stereotype is shattered the neglected facts can be 'ship-wrecked with it.' Example: progressive stereotype ignored slums, overcrowding, drift from land; in war it produced misplaced expectations of victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trained observer criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective study of actual culture requires moving 'freely among all sorts and conditions of men' and a 'trained observer' who profits by small indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Bryce cited: the trained observer has 'a flair' and can detect subtle signs. Use this as a standard for data collection: avoid relying solely on elite formulations; seek diverse, unbiassed persons and minute cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas generalize only with external, concrete embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A speculative idea penetrates general consciousness when it 'has assumed some external and concrete embodiment, or is recommended by some striking material evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bury example: the idea of Progress gained force in 1820–1850 because mechanical revolutions (railways, gas, steam) provided concrete evidence. Criterion: judge whether popular acceptance of an idea rests on tangible exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype content formed from salient material evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes (e.g., Progress) are often composed fundamentally of the salient material evidence available (e.g., mechanical inventions), which then shapes broader, sometimes erroneous, world-views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American example: mechanical growth made progress a dominant stereotype equating size/speed with excellence. Evaluate whether the kernel of a stereotype is overgeneralized from specific technological or material cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and propaganda can manufacture and spread stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Censors and propagandists can adopt, propagate, and let loose legends or atrocity tales because such fictions 'saw its value' for public morale and were useful regardless of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: German atrocity tales about Belgian priests show how authorities amplified or released stereotypes that fit pre-existing hatreds; criterion: trace origins and incentives for propagation when assessing a public belief's reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes produce compound or synthetic enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Under stress, societies often create a 'synthetic enemy' combining the external foe with internal opponents (e.g., 'the Hun in Germany and the Hun within the Gate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies a mechanism by which stereotypes expand to include domestic targets; evaluate whether hostile stereotypes are being redirected inward to settle internal conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind spots shift from edge to center as facts diverge
rubrics_metrics.description: There is always a point where the stereotype no longer fits and the blind spots move from edge of vision to center; unless critics and tolerant leaders respond, the stereotype may frustrate effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for institutional resilience: presence of critics and adaptable leadership who can sound alarm and recalibrate public frameworks when reality diverges from stereotype (example: postwar misreadings and calls for extreme peace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes contain zones of automaticism where effort ceases
rubrics_metrics.description: Within each stereotype there is a point 'where effort ceases and things happen of their own accord,' leading to unexamined assumptions (e.g., laissez-faire assumes spontaneous harmony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for parts of an ideology that assume automatic processes; these are potential failure points because they conceal costs, aims, or necessary institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific expertise limits generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness is highly specific: 'expert cavalrymen were not necessarily brilliant with trench-warfare and tanks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims based on expertise by checking domain alignment; do not overgeneralize competence from one sphere to another. Specialists can also exaggerate stereotype-driven compression of phenomena into their schemas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes/models simplify reality but risk becoming myths when generalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplified diagrams or models (e.g., economists' model of capitalist actor, entrepreneur, worker, consumer) can be useful heuristics but may be retailed until they prevail as 'the economic mythology of the day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a code or model is being used beyond its simplifying intent, leading to reading success as proof of the model; check for omitted variables and the social incentives reinforcing the model's prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment precedes evidence — perception shapes interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social judgments often 'preceded the evidence' so that the judgment contains the conclusion which the evidence is likely to confirm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize retrospective interpretation: actors describe outcomes in terms that fit pre-existing stereotypes (captains of industry explaining trusts as progress; losers seeing waste). Use methodological safeguards to separate prior belief from evidential assessment.
